title: Temporal Latency-Aware Burst Economy PRD - idea
content:
Purpose:
A lightweight PRD sketch proposing a Temporal Latency-Aware Burst Economy: an orchestration layer for Dedicated pools that blends short-term committed capacity, time-bounded burst credits, and per-tenant isolation contours to protect latency SLOs while enabling opportunistic throughput and lower cost.

Context / Problem:
- Customers buying Dedicated GPU capacity value predictability but often need headroom for short bursts (marketing spikes, jobs, retraining windows).
- Current approaches either over-provision (wasteful) or offer blunt burst models that risk noisy neighbors and latency SLO violations.
- We need a mechanism that: 1) lets tenants consume bursts without long-term cost commitments, 2) tracks and charges burst consumption fairly, and 3) enforces isolation so latency-critical tenants maintain SLOs.

Goals:
- Enable temporal bursts up to X% above committed throughput for short windows (configurable: minutes->hours).
- Maintain per-tenant latency tail SLO (e.g., P99 < configured ms) under mixed load.
- Provide clear accounting: burst credits, decay, refunding for unused prewarm, and observable economics in Console.
- Autoscaler integration: use predictive signals to pre-warm capacity when burst probability is high and gracefully fall back if unavailable.

Non-goals:
- Not a replacement for long-term reserved capacity pricing models.
- Not attempting to micro-optimize per-model kernel selection (runtime handles kernel-level perf).

High-level proposal:
1) Burst Credit Mesh: each tenant has a Burst Credit balance (minutes-of-headroom equivalent). Credits are earned via billing tiers, promotional grants, or purchased on-demand. Credits have TTL and decay curve.
2) Tempoed Commitment Gate: tenants' committed lanes are expressed as throughput per-minute. The gate permits consumption above commitment using credits but enforces a soft-failback when platform headroom is constrained.
3) Isolation Contours: define per-tenant contours (latency-critical | throughput-focused | batch) that map to enforcement policies: preemption level, queue priority, and GV (grace value) that determines how aggressively KV-cache or prefix caching is shared.
4) Autoscale Adviser: a predictive model (lightweight, rolling-window) advises pre-warm actions to convert expected burst into transient reserved slots (warm-pool). If pre-warm is unavailable, the system will: a) attempt cross-pool borrowing within same iso-zone, b) fall back to reduced fidelity model variants (if configured), or c) throttle non-critical tenants.
5) Credit Marketplace (ops-facing): an operator tool to move ephemeral credits between tenants (for scheduled events), configure grace windows, and set tenant-level credit caps.

Detailed behaviors:
- Credit consumption: tokens consumed proportionally to observed excess token-rate over committed baseline. Example: 2x baseline for 10s consumes N credits computed as excess_tokens * weight(tempo).
- Decay and refill: credits decay linearly after TTL; refill via monthly grant or on-demand purchase.
- Steady-state evictions: if cluster headroom falls below threshold and a tenant is consuming credits, we preferentially throttle credit-consuming tenants with lowest priority or highest elasticity score.
- Isolation enforcement knobs: CPU/GPU bandwidth limiters, batching window caps, queue length quotas, KV cache partitioning.

Autoscaler Integration (how it ties together):
- Input signals: tenant historical burst frequency, calendar events, product heuristics (e.g., Black Friday), model-level cost-per-token, and observed cold start rates.
- Decision: create ephemeral reservations for predicted bursts or set temporary credit rebates to encourage smoother ramps.
- Safety: autoscaler never reduces guaranteed committed capacity; only manages ephemeral warm pool and influences credit pricing.

Operational controls and observability:
- Console surfaces: per-tenant credit balance, recent credit burn timeline, projected exhaustion time, associated costs, and predicted burst odds.
- Alerts: credit exhaustion, unexpected burst > 3x baseline, isolation violations (tail latency spikes), cross-pool borrowing events.
- Runbook: automated fallback sequence (warm-pool -> cross-pool borrow -> fidelity degrade -> throttle). Include steps for on-call to engage support and manual credit moves.

Billing & economics:
- Two-part accounting: baseline committed monthly fee + burst consumption billed at on-demand rate (or discounted if purchased as bucket).
- Offer promotional credits to new customers to exercise burst flows safely.
- Provide tenant-level cost attribution and per-route token-level chargebacks in Console.

Success metrics:
- Reduction in customer-initiated long-term over-reservation (target: -20% reserved spend for pilot cohort).
- Maintain P99 latency SLO for latency-critical tenants during mixed bursts (target: <5% SLO breaches vs baseline).
- Predictive autoscaler true-positive rate for recommended pre-warms (target: 65% within pilot).
- Observability: Console adoption — 80% of pilot tenants review credit dashboards weekly.

User stories (examples):
- As a growth engineer, I want to run a targeted campaign that may double traffic for 30 minutes and not pay for an entire month of extra reserved capacity. I buy a temporary credit bundle and schedule a pre-warm.
- As a platform SRE, I want automatic isolation so that a tenant doing large batch embeddings doesn't cause P99 spikes for a latency-critical tenant sharing the same pool.
- As a product manager, I want to see projected burst costs for planned events so I can decide whether to purchase credits or accept throttling risk.

Rollout plan (sketch):
1) Internal canary: enable credit accounting and soft-throttle simulation in a limited internal dedicated pool (no billing) to validate enforcement.
2) Pilot with two customers (one latency-critical, one throughput) with manual ops support. Test cross-pool borrowing and runbooks.
3) Expand pilots, add autoscaler recommendations, expose Console panels.
4) General availability with billing integration and SLO-backed guardrails.

Open questions / risks:
- Complexity: how many contour types are manageable? Start with 3 and iterate.
- Fairness: how to avoid gaming of credit decay and refill? (proposed: anti-abuse heuristics and manual review pipeline).
- Pricing psychology: will customers accept burst pricing or prefer blunt over-provision? Need pilot feedback.
- Instrumentation cost: telemetry volume for per-token chargeback may increase cost; explore aggregated accounting windows.

Next steps / immediate TODOs:
- Engineering spike: prototype credit accounting + soft-throttle (2wk). Owner: Ethan Morales.
- Design: console mockups for credit UX and alerts. Owner: Lina Chen.
- Finance: pricing experiments and promo credit buckets. Owner: Rahul Sinha.
- Ops: draft runbooks for fallback ladder and cross-pool borrowing policy. Owner: Priya Kapoor.

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Consider decay curves that penalize burst hoarding but permit planned event reservations.
- Could map credits to a continuous numeric elasticity score used by autoscaler.
- Think about preserving prefix/KV cache locality when borrowing across pools to minimize tail latencies.
- Small batch of A/B tests to compare throttle-first vs degrade-first during shortage.

References and related tickets:
- DED-4123: experimental credit accounting prototype
- conf:DedicatedBurstEconomy design page (linked above)
- PR: dedicated-autoscaler#78 (predictive pre-warm algorithm prototype)

This is intentionally a working/brainstorm sketch — want feedback on credit math, contour taxonomy, and conservative vs aggressive fallback ordering.
